title: Humanities Exclusion
description: The humanities exclusion, IRC § 41(d)(4)(G), bars the R&D credit for research in the social sciences, arts or humanities.
summary: The humanities exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) bars U.S. taxpayers from claiming the federal R&D tax credit for research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities, including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences. Qualification turns on the scientific discipline used to resolve uncertainty, not the end product's industry.

body.text: The humanities exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) bars U.S. taxpayers from claiming the federal R&D tax credit for research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities, including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences. Qualification turns on the scientific discipline used to resolve uncertainty, not the end product's industry.
Executive Mandate and Statutory Context of the Humanities Exclusion

The Humanities Exclusion serves as a foundational statutory boundary within the United States Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit regime under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, demarcating eligible technological experimentation from disqualified inquiry in the non-natural sciences, arts, and humanities. Elaborated in Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(8), which was promulgated under Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9104 and made effective for taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, the governing regulatory provision states verbatim: Qualified research does not include research in the social sciences (including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences), arts, or humanities. By establishing an explicit subject-matter bar, Congress and the Department of the Treasury confined federal research tax subsidies to investigative activities grounded in the principles of the hard sciences—specifically the physical sciences, biological sciences, engineering, and computer science.

Under the enacted text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4), the Humanities Exclusion (Social sciences, etc.—Any research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities) is codified at IRC § 41(d)(4)(G), whereas IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) governs internal-use computer software and IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) governs foreign research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States. The regulatory implementation of IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) is codified at Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) because the Treasury Regulations consolidate several statutory provisions into distinct paragraph numbering. Because statutory authority supersedes administrative commentary or secondary summaries, all tax compliance, examination defense, and audit substantiation documentation must reference IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) alongside Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8).

Functionally, IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) operates in tandem with the "Technological Nature" requirement of the mandatory four-part test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i). Whereas IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) operates as an affirmative inclusion rule requiring that qualified research be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) operates as an explicit per se exclusion that eliminates any residual ambiguity regarding soft-science or humanistic methodologies. Even where a corporate initiative employs rigorous empirical methods, multivariable statistical modeling, or iterative hypothesis testing to achieve substantial commercial value, the activity is statutorily barred from generating Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) if the underlying uncertainty pertains to human behavior, consumer preference, market dynamics, organizational structure, financial risk, or aesthetic expression rather than physical, biological, engineering, or computer science principles. In modern interdisciplinary product development—most notably software engineering, financial technology, and digital product design—this statutory architecture necessitates strict cost segregation between excluded behavioral or economic research and qualifying technical architecture.
Foundational Framework of Qualified Research Under IRC Section 41
Legislative Purpose and Qualified Research Expenses

Enacted to stimulate domestic technological investment and overcome market underinvestment in high-risk technical innovation, IRC Section 41 provides an incremental tax credit for eligible expenditures incurred in developing or improving a "business component". Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B), a business component is statutorily defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. This business-component definition establishes the granular unit of account to which both the affirmative qualification criteria and the statutory exclusions—including the Humanities Exclusion—must be applied.

Eligible expenditures are restricted to three narrow statutory categories of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) defined under IRC § 41(b) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2. First, taxpayers may claim in-house employee wages paid or incurred for "qualified services," which encompass engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, directly supervising qualified research, or directly supporting qualified research. Second, QREs include the cost of supplies used and consumed in the conduct of qualified research, explicitly excluding land, improvements to land, and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Third, taxpayers may claim contract research expenses paid or incurred to third parties for the performance of qualified research on behalf of the taxpayer. However, even where corporate expenditures fall cleanly within these three cost categories, the underlying activities cannot generate QREs unless they satisfy the narrow statutory definition of qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(1) and avoid every categorical exclusion enumerated in IRC § 41(d)(4).
The Cumulative Four-Part Test Under IRC Section 41(d)(1)

Before evaluating specific statutory carve-outs under IRC § 41(d)(4), every research activity—applied separately to each discrete business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A)—must satisfy all four cumulative criteria established in IRC § 41(d)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2). Failure to satisfy any single prong results in immediate and total disqualification of the associated costs for that business component.

IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) explicitly disqualifies research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors, reinforcing the bar against aesthetic or artistic endeavors.

Forms the direct theoretical foundation for IRC § 41(d)(4)(G): reliance on economics, psychology, sociology, business management, arts, or humanities fails this prong.

body.text: As established in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), the routine application of existing engineering principles or the performance of basic calculations on readily available data does not establish technical uncertainty or a discovery of technological information. Rather, the investigative effort must target functional, structural, physical, biological, or algorithmic barriers that cannot be resolved through standard practice, linking the systematic testing process directly to functional capabilities rather than routine quality control, commercial validation, or production troubleshooting.

A deeper structural relationship exists across the four prongs of IRC § 41(d)(1) that explains why Congress enacted IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) as an independent statutory bar. In corporate practice, sophisticated projects in behavioral economics, quantitative market research, and organizational design frequently employ methodologies—such as randomized controlled trials, statistical simulations, and iterative hypothesis testing—that closely resemble a "process of experimentation" under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C). Absent a strict subject-matter boundary, taxpayers could argue that any systematic, data-driven evaluation of design alternatives aimed at improving product performance (defined broadly as commercial efficacy) satisfies the four-part test. By anchoring the Technological Nature test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) to the four enumerated hard-science domains and reinforcing it with the explicit Humanities Exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and the cosmetic/aesthetic exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(3)(B), the statute forecloses arguments that methodological rigor in the social sciences or humanities can substitute for hard-science experimentation.
Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Humanities Exclusion
Explicit Categories of Disqualified Disciplines

Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8), the Humanities Exclusion operates as a per se statutory bar across two overarching intellectual domains: the social sciences and the arts and humanities. This secondary statutory filter ensures that activities exhibiting high organizational rigor, advanced mathematical modeling, or systematic empirical evaluation remain barred from generating federal research tax credits if their intellectual foundation is non-technical.
Social Sciences: Economics, Business Management, and Behavioral Sciences

The regulatory definition of social sciences in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) explicitly encompasses economics, business management, and behavioral sciences alongside sociology and related human-factor disciplines. Within the domain of economics and business management, disqualified activities include the preparation and modeling of financial data, actuarial and pricing analysis, econometric forecasting, development of corporate management organization plans, and management-driven modifications to production workflows—such as rearranging assembly-line workstations or altering shift structures to improve labor throughput and communication efficiency.

In examination practice, the social sciences exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) frequently operates in tandem with the separate statutory exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(5), which disqualifies efficiency surveys, activities relating to management functions or techniques, market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), routine data collection, and routine quality control testing. When a taxpayer conducts workflow efficiency studies, organizational hierarchy restructuring, or consumer price-sensitivity modeling, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) can assert dual statutory bars under both subparagraphs (D) and (G) of IRC § 41(d)(4).

Within the domain of behavioral sciences—which encompasses cognitive and behavioral psychology, sociology, and behavioral economics—the exclusion bars research examining how individuals perceive, absorb, process, and react to stimuli, information, or non-economic behavioral drivers such as social norms and interpersonal trust. Even when behavioral studies employ rigorous statistical designs, control groups, and large-scale empirical datasets, any inquiry aimed at predicting, measuring, or influencing human preference, cognitive comfort, or user behavior fails to qualify under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8).
Arts and Humanities: Methodology Versus Application

Research directed toward historical scholarship, literary or linguistic study, philosophical inquiry, cultural analysis, fine arts, or aesthetic expression is categorically excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8). Crucially, however, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) and (c)(10) (specifically Example 9), together with the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities IRC § 41 (ATG), draw a sharp analytical distinction between the underlying scientific principles of the research process and the commercial or cultural domain of the final product.

The governing legal test examines the scientific discipline relied upon to resolve the uncertainty, not the industry or end-user market in which the resulting business component is deployed. As illustrated in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 9 and the IRS ATG, historical research into the biography, cultural context, or painting techniques of an 18th-century artist is excluded under the humanities rule. Conversely, chemical engineering or materials science research conducted to formulate a novel artist's paint pigment with improved lightfastness or structural integrity relies on the physical sciences and is therefore not excluded by IRC § 41(d)(4)(G), even though the end product serves the fine arts.

body.text: Regulatory Application in Practice: Financial Modeling and Interdisciplinary Scenarios
Analysis of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 10

The authoritative regulatory illustration of the social sciences exclusion is codified in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 10. In this example, taxpayer X, a life insurance company, undertakes a project to develop a new life insurance product. During the course of product development, X conducts systematic research across three interrelated areas: first, analyzing the effect of pricing structures and federal tax consequences on consumer demand for the life insurance product; second, modeling the expected volatility of future interest rates; and third, projecting expected mortality rates by analyzing published demographic data and prior insurance claims experience. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 10 concludes unequivocally that X's activities related to developing the new life insurance product are excluded from qualified research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) because they constitute research in the social sciences, specifically economics and business management.

The analytical significance of Example 10 lies in its rejection of quantitative complexity as a proxy for technological nature. Actuarial modeling, stochastic interest-rate forecasting, and price-elasticity estimation require substantial intellectual capital, advanced mathematical and statistical execution, and yield a novel commercial business component. Nevertheless, because the unknowns being resolved pertain to economic factors (market demand and pricing) and actuarial or business management factors (interest rate volatility and mortality risk) rather than physical, biological, engineering, or computer-science constraints, the activity is statutorily disqualified.

By contrast, if a financial institution develops a mathematically novel computer-science algorithm and system architecture for high-speed automated trading to overcome network throughput, concurrency, or memory-allocation bottlenecks, the software engineering effort targets computer-science uncertainty rather than economic forecasting. While the economic trading strategy remains excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Example 10, the underlying low-latency execution engine may qualify if all four prongs of IRC § 41(d)(1) (and, where applicable, the internal-use software requirements of IRC § 41(d)(4)(E)) are satisfied.
Interdisciplinary Boundary Scenarios
Evaluating mixed-discipline projects requires decomposing a commercial initiative into discrete technical and non-technical activities at the business-component and sub-component levels.

Evaluating pricing/tax effects on demand, interest rate volatility, and mortality rates from published data and prior claims.
Rooted in economics, actuarial science, and business management; barred by IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8).
Developing a novel low-latency algorithm and system architecture for high-speed automated order execution.
Resolves computer science uncertainty (execution speed, concurrency, algorithmic efficiency) under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i).
Designing a novel graph traversal algorithm to improve computational matching speed across large user graphs.
Uncertainty resides in computer science (graph theory and database query efficiency), not in psychological compatibility theory.
Surveying 10,000 users to determine whether blue or red interface buttons yield higher click conversion rates.
Constitutes market research (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)), psychological preference testing (IRC § 41(d)(4)(G)), and cosmetic design (IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)).

Formulating a new chemical pigment for artist's paint vs. researching the historical life of an artist.
Pigment development relies on chemistry and materials science (Qualified); biographical inquiry is humanities research (Excluded).
Designing a new organizational hierarchy or rearranging assembly workstations to improve workflow communication.
Management science and organizational restructuring are barred under both IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and IRC § 41(d)(4)(G).

body.text: A critical pattern emerges from comparing these interdisciplinary scenarios: whenever a project blends behavioral, economic, or historical subject matter with software or physical engineering, tax qualification turns on isolating the locus of uncertainty. In the dating application scenario, formulating a psychological questionnaire or sociological weighting model to predict interpersonal compatibility is behavioral science excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G). However, once those matching rules are treated as fixed mathematical inputs, engineering a novel graph-traversal indexing structure to reduce database query latency across large user graphs addresses a computer science uncertainty (graph theory and database query efficiency) that falls outside the Humanities Exclusion.
Modern Ambiguity: Behavioral Science Versus Human Factors Engineering in Digital Systems
The Friction Point in User Experience (UX) and Human-Computer Interaction (HCI)

The most acute compliance friction under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) arises in contemporary software development, where User Experience (UX), User Interface (UI), and Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) teams operate alongside systems engineers. Because digital products mediate between computational architectures and human operators, developmental testing frequently involves human subjects. Whether such activities fall within the Humanities Exclusion depends entirely on the nature of the uncertainty being resolved.

When UX or UI testing is conducted to optimize layout aesthetics, visual convenience, cognitive comfort, or commercial conversion rates—where the underlying software architecture is already technically capable of executing any of the proposed interface alternatives—the activity is statutorily disqualified. Determining whether users respond more favorably to a specific onboarding sequence, typography, or button placement and color relies on principles of psychology, behavioral economics, and marketing (excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and (G)) as well as style, taste, or cosmetic design factors (excluded under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)). In these instances, the technical capability of the software system is never in doubt; the only uncertainty is human preference.

Conversely, Human Factors Engineering (HFE) can satisfy the four-part test when empirical testing of the human-machine interface is intrinsically necessary to resolve a technical uncertainty regarding the functional capability, reliability, or structural design of the underlying hardware or software architecture. For example, in engineering a real-time control interface for surgical robotics, a virtual reality simulation environment, or a high-speed data visualization platform, engineers may face fundamental uncertainty regarding the maximum end-to-end visual latency, minimum frame-rate stability, or display bandwidth that a human operator can tolerate without compromising system performance or reliability. When human-in-the-loop testing is executed to define the quantitative engineering parameters—such as rendering pipeline architecture, packet compression algorithms, or sensor refresh thresholds—required to ensure operational capability within human sensory-processing limits, the uncertainty being resolved is rooted in computer science and systems engineering rather than behavioral psychology.

This statutory boundary creates a notable policy tension in the modern digital economy. A substantial share of commercial value in consumer software and financial technology derives from sophisticated applications of behavioral and psychological principles that enhance utility and drive user adoption. Because IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) enforce a strict hard-science threshold, the regulatory framework creates a policy barrier against subsidizing behavioral innovation, regardless of how novel, data-intensive, or commercially transformative that behavioral optimization may be.
Compliance Substantiation, Cost Segregation, and Audit Risk Mitigation
Burden of Proof and Examination Exposure

Under federal tax law, the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proving entitlement to all claimed QREs and demonstrating that no claimed expenditures derive from activities excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4). Heightened IRS examination scrutiny, formal disclosure requirements on updated tax forms, and recent judicial decisions denying R&D credits to engineering and design firms for inadequate substantiation underscore that merely presenting the eventual technical solution is legally insufficient. Taxpayers must maintain contemporaneous project documentation establishing a direct technical nexus between specific employee wage hours, supply costs, and contractor invoices and the iterative resolution of hard-science technical uncertainties, while meticulously tracking and excluding employee time spent on market research, efficiency surveys, cosmetic design, or psychological studies.

By contrast, claims heavily weighted toward economics (15% sustained) or psychology (5% sustained) experience severe disallowances upon IRS examination, where the small sustained percentages represent only isolated software engineering or physical product design hours that can be segregated from the disqualified social-science inquiry.
Interaction Between the "Substantially All" Rule and IRC Section 41(d)(4) Exclusions

A frequent compliance error involves misinterpreting the "substantially all" rule codified under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the requirement that "substantially all" of a taxpayer's research activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose is satisfied if 80% or more of the taxpayer's research activities for that business component (measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis) constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose.

Crucially, however, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide explicitly stipulate that the remaining balance of research activities (up to 20%) qualifies under the "substantially all" umbrella only if those remaining activities are not otherwise excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4). Consequently, activities falling under the Humanities Exclusion (IRC § 41(d)(4)(G)), market research (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)), or any other IRC § 41(d)(4) exclusion can never be swept into QREs via the 80% rule. Regardless of how minor their cost is relative to the overall project, all activities falling under the Humanities Exclusion must be strictly carved out prior to computing the credit.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Cost Segregation and the 80% "Substantially All" Rule

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) and IRC § 41(d)(4)(G), consider a hypothetical software development project (Project Alpha) in which a taxpayer incurs $500,000 in total project wage expenditures across four tracked activity buckets during the taxable year. The table below details the four expenditure buckets, their statutory classification, and the resulting QRE eligibility.

cells: Qualifying process of experimentation in computer science under IRC § 41(d)(1).
Bucket 2: Human Factors Engineering for System Latency
Qualifying physiological latency testing necessary to resolve rendering engine uncertainty under IRC § 41(d)(1).
Bucket 3: Non-Excluded Technical Support & Routine Integration
Non-experimentation technical activity not excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4); eligible via 80% rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6).
Bucket 4: Behavioral UX Preference & Pricing Elasticity Study
Disqualified behavioral psychology and economic market research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and (D); mandatory carve-out.

body.text: In the first step of the statutory computation, the taxpayer aggregates the qualifying process-of-experimentation costs from Bucket 1 ($365,000) and Bucket 2 ($45,000), yielding $410,000:
Qualifying Experimentation Costs = $365,000 + $45,000 = $410,000

In the second step, to evaluate the 80% "substantially all" threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the taxpayer divides the Qualifying Experimentation Costs ($410,000) by the Total Project Costs ($500,000):
Experimentation Ratio = $410,000 ÷ $500,000 = 0.82 = 82.0%

Because 82.0% ≥ 80.0%, the business component satisfies the "substantially all" threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). In the third step, the taxpayer evaluates the remaining 18.0% ($90,000) of project expenditures against the mandatory exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(4). Bucket 3 ($30,000, or 6.0%) consists of non-excluded technical activities; because the 80% threshold is met and Bucket 3 is not barred by IRC § 41(d)(4), this $30,000 is included in QREs under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). Conversely, Bucket 4 ($60,000, or 12.0%) consists of behavioral science and economic market research excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and (D). Even though the project met the 80% threshold, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) explicitly bars any IRC § 41(d)(4) excluded activity from qualifying. Thus, the $60,000 must be carved out and disallowed, resulting in final eligible QREs of $440,000 (88.0% of project costs) and disallowed excluded costs of $60,000 (12.0% of project costs):
Disallowed Excluded Costs = $500,000 − $440,000 = $60,000 (12.0%)
Regulatory Clarification and Policy Harmonization Recommendations
1. Updated Treasury Regulation Examples for UX/UI and Human-Computer Interaction

The current regulatory examples in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(10) (promulgated in final form in T.D. 9104 for taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003) address traditional industrial and financial scenarios—such as artist's paint formulation versus biography (Example 9) and life insurance actuarial modeling (Example 10)—but do not directly address modern Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) or UX/UI engineering. Treasury and the IRS should promulgate supplemental regulatory examples under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(10) that explicitly differentiate between disqualified psychological or aesthetic research—such as empirical studies of color theory, text layout, or user journey preferences aimed at improving commercial adoption or conversion rates under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)—and qualifying human factors engineering where human physiological or sensory interaction is the subject of technical uncertainty resolution, such as minimizing visual latency in a virtual reality or robotic teleoperation system to comply with sensory-processing limits required for system reliability under IRC § 41(d)(1).
2. Objective Examination Standards in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide

Field examiners frequently lack uniform technical criteria for evaluating interdisciplinary software teams, leading either to overbroad disallowance of legitimate systems engineering or improper allowance of behavioral marketing studies. The IRS should update its Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (IRC § 41) to establish objective evidentiary metrics distinguishing Applied Human Factors Engineering from excluded Behavioral Sciences. Specifically, the revised ATG should instruct examiners to verify whether project documentation demonstrates that human-factors testing was conducted to resolve a system-level technical failure inherent in the system's design (such as system stability, data processing speed, or algorithmic efficiency) rather than evaluating consumer preference or organizational workflow.
3. Harmonization Between IRC Section 41(d)(4)(G) and IRC Section 174 R&E Rules
The interaction between the Section 41 research credit and IRC Section 174 Research and Experimental (R&E) expenditure rules presents a major compliance concern.

Under existing Section 174 regulations (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6)), research in connection with literary, historical, or similar projects is already excluded from the definition of "research or experimental expenditures" under Section 174, yet taxpayers face administrative uncertainty during audits when interdisciplinary activities are disallowed under IRC § 41(d)(4). Such guidance will ensure that commercial and managerial research costs remain immediately deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC § 162, preventing the dual compliance penalty of losing the IRC § 41 tax credit while simultaneously suffering mandatory five-year amortization under IRC § 174.

Establish bright-line regulatory criteria separating aesthetic/preference optimization (IRC § 41(d)(4)(G)) from hardware/software technical uncertainty resolution (IRC § 41(d)(1)).
Publish an updated IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) clarifying Applied Human Factors Engineering versus Behavioral Sciences.
Provide field examiners and taxpayers with objective documentation standards tied to system-level engineering constraints.
Issue administrative guidance explicitly confirming that activities excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) are not IRC § 174 R&E expenditures.
Prevent dual compliance penalties (denial of the IRC § 41 credit coupled with mandatory five-year amortization under IRC § 174) and confirm immediate deductibility under IRC § 162.
